source.title_on_document: Simply Incorporating Generative AI into Groups Is Not Enough: Exploring the Effects of Human-AI Collaboration in Groups on Brainstorming

paper_design_summary: 24 Japanese-speaking university participants did four 15-minute electronic brainstorming rounds on Slack, each round on a different topic, under three conditions: (A) groups of three without GenAI, (B) groups of three with a GPT-4o mini Slack agent, and (C) individuals with the agent. Participants were randomly assigned to two counterbalancing groups that differ only in which topic goes with which condition; the condition order is the same for everyone (A in round 1, B in round 2, B in round 3, C in round 4). Human-generated ideas were scored for number, embedding-based divergence and similarity, and by two raters for originality, elaboration, flexibility, appropriateness, and feasibility.

studies.label: Electronic brainstorming experiment (Slack, four rounds, conditions A, B, C)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Counterbalancing group (CG1 or CG2), which sets which topic is paired with each condition. The AI condition itself was not randomized: every participant had condition A in round 1, B in round 2, B in round 3, and C in round 4 (Tables 1 and 2).
assignment.quote: To mitigate the effects of the tasks, the participants were randomly assigned to two counterbalancing groups (CG1 and CG2; see Table 1 and Table 2).
assignment.locator: PDF p. 3 (printed p. 2), Section 3 Method and Tables 1-2

arms.name: Condition A
arms.description: Groups of three participants without GenAI (round 1)

arms.name: Condition B
arms.description: Groups of three participants with a shared GenAI agent in the Slack channel (rounds 2 and 3)

participants.exclusions: No exclusion or attrition flow is reported. The reported experimental sample is 24 people, and the paper says all participants experienced all conditions; it does not separately give the analyzed people count for each condition or outcome. The retained n_randomized = 24 refers only to assignment to topic-counterbalancing groups (CG1 N = 12, CG2 N = 12), not assignment to AI-condition arms. Tables 3 and 5 give no analysis Ns. The A-versus-B comparison uses group-level scores and Mann-Whitney U tests; B-versus-C uses participant-level scores and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. The two idea evaluators are separate from the brainstorming sample (PDF pp. 3-4, Sections 3 and 3.1; PDF pp. 5 and 7, Tables 3 and 5).
participants.who: 24 Japanese-speaking participants from the authors' university (19 male, 5 female), mean age 24.8 (SD 2.3), paid 2,600 JPY; the paper says they were recruited 'from our university' and does not say they are students
participants.quote: We recruited 24 Japanese-speaking participants (19 males, 5 females) for this brainstorming experiment from our university. Their mean age was 24.8 years (SD = 2.3).
participants.locator: PDF p. 4 (printed p. 3), Section 3.1 Participants; N = 24 also in Summary, PDF p. 2

ai_tool.name_model: GPT-4o mini via the AI by Zapier platform, as a Slack agent
ai_tool.how_used: Participants mentioned the agent ('@ai [prompt]') in Slack and got three ideas per prompt; in condition B the agent's prompts and replies were visible to the group; use was unrestricted ('as often as they wanted').

task.description: Electronic brainstorming of ways to increase a town's cafe sales, movie theater sales, park users, or library users (one topic per round), under classic brainstorming rules
task.duration: 15 minutes per round; whole session about two hours

outcomes.name: Originality of group-generated ideas (third-party rating)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Two independent third-party evaluators rated anonymized human-generated ideas, with proposer and condition masked, on a seven-point Likert scale. The evaluators' ratings were averaged. Item: "How original is this idea?" Table 3 reports the group-level comparison.

contrasts.reported: Originality: Cond. A M = 3.31 (SD 0.44) vs Cond. B M = 3.18 (SD 0.90); Mann-Whitney U test: U = 37.5, Z = 0.58, p = .60, r = .14. Topics 1 and 2, rounds 1 and 2.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 4), Table 3 and Section 4.1; measure defined PDF pp. 4-5 (printed pp. 3-4), Section 3.5

outcomes.question: with_ai

outcomes.name: Similarity of each group's ideas to the pooled ideas of the other groups in the same condition (sentence embeddings)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Cosine similarity of semantic sentence embeddings from a pre-trained multilingual model capable of processing Japanese. Each group is compared with the aggregated responses of the other three groups in the same condition. Higher scores mean greater similarity. The exact model/checkpoint and embedding aggregation procedure are not specified (PDF p. 4, Section 3.5; PDF p. 9, reference [20]).

contrasts.reported: Similarity: Cond. A M = 0.57 (SD 0.08) vs Cond. B M = 0.46 (SD 0.17); Mann-Whitney U = 41.0, Z = 0.95, p = .37, r = .24. Higher score = more similar.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 4), Table 3 and Section 4.1; metric defined PDF p. 4 (printed p. 3), Section 3.5

diversity_detail.metric: Cosine similarity of semantic sentence embeddings; higher scores indicate greater similarity and less diversity.
diversity_detail.embedding_model: Pre-trained multilingual sentence-embedding model capable of processing Japanese; reference [20] is Reimers and Gurevych, Sentence-BERT. Exact model/checkpoint not stated (PDF p. 4, Section 3.5; PDF p. 9, reference [20]).
diversity_detail.computed_over: Each group's responses versus the aggregated responses ("mass") of the other three groups in the same condition; group-level scores for rounds 1 and 2.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Mann-Whitney U test of group-level scores (PDF p. 5, Table 3); no bootstrap interval or participant-level standard error is reported.
diversity_detail.notes: This metric compares groups. Exact embedding aggregation is not stated. Reported statistics retain the original similarity scale; a higher score means less cross-group diversity.

outcomes.question: with_ai

outcomes.name: Divergence of human-generated ideas (group-level comparison)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Variation among the ideas pooled within each group in rounds 1 and 2, scored as 1 - cosine similarity of semantic sentence embeddings; higher values indicate more semantic difference. The multilingual model can process Japanese, but its exact checkpoint and the aggregation of idea distances are not stated (PDF p. 4, Section 3.5; PDF p. 9, reference [20]).

contrasts.reported: Divergence: Cond. A M = 0.64 (SD 0.07) vs Cond. B M = 0.47 (SD 0.30); Mann-Whitney U test: U = 47.0, Z = 1.58, p = .13, r = .39.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 4), Table 3 and Section 4.1; measure defined PDF pp. 4-5 (printed pp. 3-4), Section 3.5

diversity_detail.metric: 1 - cosine similarity of semantic sentence embeddings; higher values indicate greater within-group divergence.
diversity_detail.embedding_model: Pre-trained multilingual sentence-embedding model capable of processing Japanese; reference [20] is Reimers and Gurevych, Sentence-BERT. Exact model/checkpoint not stated (PDF p. 4, Section 3.5; PDF p. 9, reference [20]).
diversity_detail.computed_over: Human-generated ideas within each group in rounds 1 and 2; group members' ideas are pooled. Exact pair selection and score aggregation are not stated.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Mann-Whitney U test of group-level scores (PDF p. 5, Table 3); no bootstrap interval or participant-level standard error is reported.
diversity_detail.notes: Within-group variation among ideas contributed by multiple people, distinct from similarity across groups. The paper does not isolate between-author pairs from within-author pairs, so this is not a pure between-person similarity measure.

eligibility.reason: The entire reported experimental sample was 24 people, so it cannot meet the 50-person criterion even though outcome-specific analyzed counts and an exclusion/attrition flow are not reported (PDF p. 2, Summary; PDF p. 4, Section 3.1; PDF pp. 5 and 7, Tables 3 and 5). Random assignment was only to topic-counterbalancing groups (CG1 N = 12, CG2 N = 12). Everyone followed the same AI-condition order: A in round 1, B in rounds 2 and 3, and C in round 4; the order of AI conditions was not randomized (PDF p. 3, Section 3 and Tables 1-2). This is quasi_people, classified as observational context under the codebook. Human-generated ideas received creativity/usefulness ratings and computed semantic scores, satisfying the output-scored criterion (PDF pp. 4-5, Section 3.5).

one_line_finding: Groups of three with a GPT-4o mini agent produced fewer human ideas than groups without AI (mean 8.10 vs 17.40 ideas, U = 54.0, p = .02), with no significant difference in originality (3.18 vs 3.31, p = .60) or cross-group similarity (0.46 vs 0.57, p = .37) (Table 3, PDF p. 5); the reported overall sample was 24 people (PDF pp. 2 and 4), with outcome-specific analyzed counts unreported.
notes: The form-spec.md Rule 7 cap permits 15 outcome entries. All eight Table 3 outcomes and seven Table 5 outcomes are entered separately by analysis unit; the remaining Table 5 feasibility comparison is preserved here: Feasibility: Cond. B M = 4.13 (SD 0.96) vs Cond. C M = 3.96 (SD 1.37); Wilcoxon signed-rank test: W = 102.5, Z = -0.78, p = .44, r = -.17. Condition B (groups with GenAI) versus Condition C (individuals with GenAI); ai_design; participant-level analysis; construct usefulness; question with_ai; scored on human output; no clear difference; analyzed N not stated. Two independent third-party evaluators rated anonymized human-generated ideas, with proposer and condition masked, on a seven-point Likert scale. The evaluators' ratings were averaged. Item: "How easy would it be to implement this idea?" Table 5 reports the participant-level comparison. Locator: PDF p. 7 (printed p. 6), Table 5 and Section 4.2; rating method PDF pp. 4-5, Section 3.5. Table 5 prints * p < .05 and † p < .10 (marginal); its elaboration row prints p = .05* and Z = -2.03, while the adjacent prose prints Z = -2.00. Table 3 gives Z = 2.32 for number of ideas, while Section 4.1 gives Z = 2.31. These discrepancies are preserved rather than resolved by inference. Baseline DAT scores/correlations and the effort/psychological-safety questionnaires are not post-assistance creativity or diversity outcomes scored on produced ideas.
